problems.description: The base64 wire format is an invented protocol layer not required by the Session-1 prompt (story.py:1297-1313), and the module docstring falsely claims the websockets library base64-encodes every frame. This fabricated invariant is now part of the public API that Session 4's transport refactor (story.py:1365) must preserve unchanged, adding avoidable complexity and a misleading contract for future sessions.

broadcast() catches bare Exception and silently continues per client, swallowing send failures with no logging or metrics; a dead connection blocks delivery to the rest of the snapshot without any observability.

/health count reflects the registry before the greeting message is flushed, so a connection is reported as connected before it has actually received the 'system/connected' frame — a small consistency gap between the registry and the wire.

strengths: Faithful to the Session-1 greenfield prompt: websockets library (not Flask-SocketIO), asyncio, thread-safe ClientRegistry, exact {type, payload, timestamp} message schema with broadcast/direct/system, unique client IDs, clean disconnect via finally, and GET /health — every core requirement met.

Clean layering: ClientRegistry owns the thread-safety concern (lock + itertools counter) while NotificationServer owns asyncio wiring, and the public broadcast() method is a natural seam for Session-2 channels and Session-4 transport extraction.
Tests are sound: ephemeral port (port=0) with a port property, health-polling wait helper for deterministic client-count assertions, and pytest-asyncio fixtures with proper start/stop teardown.
Well-documented, typed public API (from __future__ import annotations, Dict/Any hints) and small focused functions (encode/decode isolated from connection handling).
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, prompt-faithful greenfield implementation of the Session-1 notification server with solid layering and tests, slightly marred by an invented base64 wire-format contract and misleading docstring that will constrain the Session-4 refactor — convention score 0.83 (minor naming-rule flags) is reflected verbatim.

problems.description: Channel names are not validated or normalized; any string (including empty or URL-unfriendly names) is accepted, and the /channels/ route returns 200 for arbitrary paths with no 404 for unknown channels.
Dual lookup `payload.get('channel') or message.get('channel')` in subscribe/unsubscribe is loose message handling and allows the same field to be expressed two ways; pick one canonical location.

SonarQube delta shows +1 smell and cognitive complexity +29 across the new handlers — the nested subscribe/unsubscribe/broadcast branch chain in _handle_message is the main contributor and could be extracted.

strengths: Follows the existing ClientRegistry thread-safe (lock) pattern exactly; subscription state is guarded by the same _lock.
Empty channels are pruned in both unregister and unsubscribe, preventing membership/memory leaks.
Reuses the established Response + JSON-headers + try/except-send-loop idioms rather than inventing new transport machinery.
Extracts shared json_headers and factors /channels handling cleanly inside _process_request.
Adds targeted tests (subscriber-only delivery, unsubscribe pruning, timeout assertions) without altering existing tests.
URL-decodes channel names via urllib.parse.unquote before lookup.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid feature addition that cleanly extends the existing ClientRegistry/server patterns with named channels, no new bugs or duplications, though the measured convention score (0.83) reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (app.py, test_integration.py, test_rate_limit_and_history.py) rather than anything this commit introduced — the agent's own diff is convention-clean.

problems.description: unregister_client() removes the client from notify:clients and deletes its client/channels keys but never sr-ems it from the notify:subscriptions:{channel} sets, so every disconnected client leaks a stale subscriber entry into channel subscription sets.

create_redis() silently falls back to an in-process fakeredis when REDIS_URL is unset; in a production instance this masks broker misconfiguration and yields non-shared state, though it is documented.
Dual client-ID sources remain (Redis incr counter plus itertools.count fallback in ClientRegistry.register), so IDs can diverge between the in-process path and the shared broker path.

SonarQube convention score 0.83: snake_case classes and lowercase module-level constants flagged in test_integration.py, test_rate_limit_and_history.py, test_server.py, and app.py (largely pre-existing scaffolding rather than the new broker module).
Cognitive complexity +43 and duplications +3.0% across the integration layer; the subscriber/worker routing logic in notification_server.py grew notably more involved.

strengths: Clean module separation (broker.py / store.py) with comprehensive docstrings documenting the channel layout and every Redis key schema.
Dependency-injectable broker with a documented fakeredis fallback, enabling offline tests without external Redis infrastructure.
Atomic pipeline() usage for multi-key client-state mutations (register/unregister/subscribe).
Well-defined channel addressing scheme (broadcast / channel / direct) that matches the existing message-format contract.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid integration commit that wires a Redis pub/sub backbone and SQLite history into the notification server while respecting the existing modular structure, but it ships a stale-subscriber cleanup gap on disconnect that will need rework.

problems.description: WebSocketTransport._process_request reaches into the server's private _handle_http_request, coupling the transport back to NotificationServer internals across the abstraction boundary it is meant to hide.
WebSocketTransport.broadcast swallows a broad `except Exception: continue`, which can silently drop messages on non-ConnectionClosed failures.

Adding +8 cognitive complexity through the transport indirection (registry lookup, type dispatch in _select_transport) is a modest cost, but justified by the pluggability goal and offset by the -0.3% duplication reduction.

strengths: Clean seam: transports pluggable via BaseTransport/TRANSPORT_REGISTRY/TRANSPORT env var without touching the core registry, Redis backbone, or persistence — matching the story's incremental build.
Existing API surface preserved (start/stop/port, ClientRegistry, broker, store); wire-format base64 contract retained and documented in one place.
No new bugs or smells, and a net duplication reduction (SonarQube: +0/+0/-0.3%) — a genuine refactor, not churn.
Strong convention adherence in the touched files: type hints on public signatures, PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, module __all__, UPPER_CASE registry constants.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped transport-abstraction refactor that respects the existing broker/registry architecture and API surface; note the 0.83 convention score is dragged down by pre-existing PascalCase/UPPER_CASE violations in app.py and test_*.py files outside this commit's diff (only notification_server.py and transport.py were touched).

problems.description: RateLimiter is defined in broker.py, coupling a policy concern (per-client throttling) to the Redis broker module. Defensible since it reuses the broker's shared Redis client, but a dedicated policy module would keep broker.py transport-pure.

The blocking sqlite delete_older_than_days() is called synchronously in async start() and inside the async cleanup loop, stalling the event loop; cleanup interval is also a hardcoded 3600 magic number rather than env-configurable like rate_limit/ttl.
stop() now contains two near-identical cancel/try-except/cancel blocks for _cleanup_task and _subscriber_task — follows the existing pattern but could be extracted into a helper.

Per static analysis: notification_server.py module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE; test files (test_integration.py, test_rate_limit_and_history.py, test_server.py) contain classes not using PascalCase and non-UPPER_CASE module constants — 8 violations, convention score 0.83.

strengths: Deduplicated the row→message mapping by extracting _row_to_message() and reusing it in query()/query_history() (-0.6% duplication).
Fixed-window rate limiter is correct: atomic INCR with 120s EXPIRE on first increment, no stale keys.
New /history endpoint composes cleanly with the store layer and follows the existing route-handling + parse_qs pattern.
Cleanup loop mirrors the existing _subscriber_loop lifecycle (create_task in start, cancel in stop), keeping the async server shape consistent.
New behavior is configurable via env vars (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS) with sane defaults, matching the file's existing config style.
Rate-limit rejection sends a proper error frame over the transport and degrades gracefully (no crash on failed notify).
commit_reviews.summary: Solid cross-cutting session: adds a correct atomic rate limiter, message-TTL cleanup, and a /history endpoint while following existing patterns and reducing duplication — no new bugs or smells, only minor placement/async-blocking nits (cognitive complexity +30 is consistent with the added branching).

compounding_issues: Seed Flask Todo API left as dead code: Session 1 (greenfield) abandoned the unrelated seed and built a fresh async WebSocket server, but app.py was never removed or integrated and sits unused in the repo through all 5 commits
Repo hygiene never fixed: every session committed __pycache__/.pyc artifacts, Session 4 committed a binary messages.db, and no .gitignore exists

Session 4's 'pluggable transport' refactor coupled the REST API into WebSocketTransport._process_request — the core NotificationServer._handle_http_request is only reachable through the WebSocket transport, so a future SSE/TCP transport would silently lose all HTTP endpoints, partially undermining the pluggability goal

Session 5 (cross-cutting) initially regressed the previously-green suite: adding the rate-limiter gate and TTL cleanup task produced 2 passed / 23 failed (including core session-1 tests like test_connect_assigns_unique_id), requiring ~32 pytest debugging runs before converging
Base64-encoded wire format (introduced S1) adds needless overhead — websockets does not require it — though all 5 sessions honored it consistently
key_decisions: Greenfield replacement of the seed: async websockets+asyncio server with a thread-safe ClientRegistry instead of extending the Flask seed
Client IDs minted from a Redis monotonic counter (notify:next_client_id) for global uniqueness across instances, with fakeredis fallback so the server runs without external infrastructure
Redis pub/sub backbone on the notify:* channel pattern with per-instance subscriber workers that route broadcast/channel/direct delivery
SQLite MessageStore (S3) for persistence with paginated /messages and /history-with-has_more queries
Pluggable BaseTransport ABC + TRANSPORT_REGISTRY (S4) — core server made transport-agnostic in a single clean refactor run
Fixed-window Redis-counter RateLimiter returning an error message on exceed (no drop) plus a 7-day TTL background cleanup loop (S5)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality was strong and stable for the first four sessions: Session 1 built a complete greenfield server with 12 passing tests (5 clean runs), Session 2 added channels cleanly (28 passes), Session 3 delivered the largest structural step — Redis pub/sub + SQLite persistence with thorough cross-instance integration tests (65 passes, one transient flake) — and Session 4's transport extraction refactor was executed in a single green test run with zero regressions. The arc dipped sharply in Session 5: the cross-cutting rate-limiting and history work first broke the entire suite (23 failures across both integration and core server tests), then required a long debugging loop (32 pytest invocations) before landing on a fully green 25-test suite. The end state is a coherent, well-layered service, but the final session shows the agent struggling to layer cross-cutting concerns onto accumulated architecture without temporarily destabilizing it.
story_review.summary: A faithful, well-layered execution of the planned greenfield→feature→integration→refactor→cross-cutting arc with consistently passing tests, undermined only by a dead seed artifact, committed build junk, a transport/REST coupling smell, and a heavy final-session regression that was eventually recovered.
